reports.title: Review: The Shimano Nexave Heralds a New Era of Affordability and Reliability
reports.text:
I truly enjoy a good spinning reel that won’t break the bank. Something I don’t have to spend a ton of money and can get a few years out of. Something I can hand to clients and not worry about. A reel that packs a punch, has a good drag, and can handle larger fish like pike, walleye, and musky.
I know what you’re thinking: Something like that doesn’t exist. To get all those qualities in a reel, you’ve got to be spending some serious money. But, in reality, you don’t. I’ve been a huge fan of Shimano reels my whole life. They are strong, reliable, and have the perfect balance of power and finesse. reports.title: Even as Technology Evolves, the Jig Still Earns Its Place in Your Tackle Box
reports.text:
It’s abundantly clear that forward-facing sonar has reshaped the landscape of bass fishing. And it’s not the only force changing things, as myriad new baits and techniques have dominated these past few years. However, forward-facing sonar (FFS) has not ended more traditional forms of fishing, and these fancy new baits have not rendered all old baits ineffective. In fact, the modern bait emergence has shifted the focus off some classic fish catchers. That provides a pathway for specialists to reemerge.
No bait has weathered the LIVE sonar storm better than the jig. And no one is better with a jig than Greg Hackney. Here’s his take on why this timeless fish-catcher still gets bites today.

reports.title: Transformed Troy University program on verge of best season ever
reports.text:
Four years ago, when Avery Padgett arrived at Troy University as a freshman, the Trojans had just five anglers on the roster and sent two boats to compete in a handful of events. Now, they send eight or nine teams to at least a dozen events per year across various trails.

reports.title: The Largemouth Bass With Some of the Longest-Standing State Records
reports.text:
What are your odds of catching a state-record largemouth bass?
In states such as Georgia, Michigan, and Wisconsin, not great. Those states, plus a few others, all boast state records that have been standing for more than 65 years. Are they the untouchables? Well, it would take one freak of a bass in those states to be reeled into the record books.
Let’s look at some of the oldest state records.
Georgia: 22 Pounds, 4 Ounces; Set in 1932
When George Perry and his friend J.E. Page traveled to the Ocmulgee River on June 2, 1932, they didn’t have giant bass in mind. They were simply trying to catch food for the dinner table.

reports.title: North Carolina’s George cruises to victory at Phoenix Bass Fishing League Regional on the Potomac River
reports.text:
MARBURY, Md. – Boater Andrew George of Poplar Branch, North Carolina, caught a three-day total of 15 bass weighing 47 pounds, 13 ounces, to win the Phoenix Bass Fishing League (BFL) Presented by T-H Marine Regional on the Potomac River. reports.title: Fall Crappie 101: It’s Nothing Like Fishing the Other Seasons
reports.text:
Fall is finally here, and it brings an entirely different way to target crappie. Gone are the days of 90-degree heat and a bite you have to work for. Something changes when the first cool front blows through: Crappie go from finicky to aggressive almost overnight. It happens the same way every year, all across the country.
I saw it play out again on my last trip up the Tickfaw River here in Southeast Louisiana. I was idling the main river, watching my side scan in about 20 feet of water, not looking for anything specific. Then I saw it. A brush pile with a shad ball hovering over it. Underneath were 15 blips on the screen.

reports.title: Success Lake fell to 11 percent of capacity, and fishing was hit or miss
reports.text: Bass chased shad in the evenings, and anglers who located boiling fish loaded up using crankbaits, jerkbaits, and topwater lures.

reports.title: The lake fell to 11 percent of capacity, and spotted bass fishing improved
reports.text: The lake fell to 11 percent of capacity, and spotted bass fishing improved. Bass anglers found success with finesse plastics, crankbaits, and jerkbaits. Most of the spotted bass action came from main lake points and submerged rock piles.

reports.title: Fishing was good in the southern aqueduct
reports.text: Fishing was good in the southern aqueduct, as striped bass, largemouth bass, and catfish consistently took various baits. Largemouth bass struck topwater poppers and Spook Jr.'s in baitfish and bone colors at first light and again during the evenings, while wacky-rigged YUM Dingers fished on a jig head successfully fooled bass positioned near inlets and concrete bridge pylons.

Matching your jig to the size and shape of the main crappie forage can greatly increase your number of hookups.
Crappie Basics: Match the Hatch for More Crappie
By Keith Sutton
One of the simplest ways to improve your crappie fishing is to give the fish what they’re already looking for. That means matching your jig to the size and general shape of the forage crappie are feeding on.
If 2-inch minnows make up a big part of the crappie diet in the lake you’re fishing, for example, a 2-inch jig is a logical choice. If the fish are eating tiny shiners, you’ll probably do better with a smaller offering. The same principle applies when shad, fathead minnows or other forage dominate the menu.

reports.title: How To: Hot Summertime Tactics for catching crappie
reports.text:
Hot Summertime Tactics for Catching Crappie
When summer water gets hot, crappie usually leave the shallow cover and seek cooler, more oxygenated water, shade, and baitfish. The key is finding where those conditions overlap.
Fish deeper: Start around 15–30 feet, then adjust based on your lake’s depth and thermocline. Electronics are extremely helpful for locating suspended schools.
Target brush piles: Deep brush, submerged trees, and man-made structure can hold crappie throughout summer. Slowly work a jig vertically around the cover.
Follow the bait: Find schools of shad or other forage and look nearby—and often directly beneath them—for crappie.

reports.title: Product Buzz, by Scott Mackenthun
reports.text:
Northland Tackle Deep Vee Spin Jig
Northland’s underspin jig, the Deep Vee Spin, is a catcher. Cast it or troll it and you’ll catch fish. This jig shines in crystal clear waters where its flashy willow blade makes all the difference in getting fish’s attention and getting bit. The jig has a keeled body shape to help it fall fast and track straight. Built into the design is a wire keeper that ensures plastics stay snug on the hook shank. Try the 1/8 or 1/16th ounce for crappies. MSRP $8 for a two pack.
